Who collects property tax in Waukesha County?

It depends on your municipality: some communities collect the first installment themselves, and others have contracted with the Waukesha County Treasurer to do it. The treasurer's office is in Room AC148 of the Administration Building, 515 W. Moreland Blvd., Waukesha, WI 53188. The phone is 262-548-7029, and the office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday.

The county treasurer collects the second installment everywhere and takes delinquent payments. According to the treasurer's page, you can pay by mail, in the blue and white drive-up drop box on the east side of the Administration Building, or online. Anything deposited in the drop box by 7:30 a.m. is dated the previous day.

What are the property tax due dates in Waukesha County communities?

Most Waukesha County municipalities use January 31 and July 31, but a few allow three payments. The county's tax due date chart shows the pattern.

Three-payment schedules come from a local ordinance, which Wis. Stat. 74.12 allows. Under that statute at least half the tax must be paid by April 30 and everything by July 31. If you pay in installments and miss one, the entire unpaid balance goes delinquent, so check your bill rather than assuming the standard schedule.

Which Waukesha County communities pay the county for the first installment?

The county has agreements with a group of municipalities, so a first-installment check for one of them goes to the Waukesha County Treasurer. Per the county's note to mortgage companies and escrow agents, the list includes the Town of Brookfield, City of Delafield, Town of Delafield, and the villages of Dousman, Elm Grove, Lannon, Lisbon, Menomonee Falls, Merton, Nashotah, North Prairie, Oconomowoc Lake, Pewaukee, Wales and Waukesha.

Everyone else pays the local treasurer first. The county does not receive tax information from the City of Waukesha until the first of the following year, so ask that city's treasurer for amounts. Tax data for most other communities appears on the county's online tax lookup through December.

What happens when Waukesha County taxes are late?

Late taxes grow by 1.5 percent a month, counted from February 1. The county's glossary splits that into 1 percent interest and a 0.5 percent penalty, both computed on the unpaid balance on the first business day of each month.

The county handles delinquency in a set order:

  • Tax statements showing delinquent taxes, interest and penalty are mailed in February and August.
  • On September 1 the county issues a tax certificate for every property with unpaid current-year tax, which acts as a lien in the county's favor.
  • The certificate must be held for two years before foreclosure can start.
  • The in rem process under Wis. Stat. 75.521 adds in rem fees, and an owner must pay all taxes, specials, interest, penalties and those fees to redeem.

The treasurer's page also advertises tax foreclosure auctions run through WisconsinSurplus.com. If you owe more than one year, ask the treasurer for a written payoff before you list or sign a contract.

Does a postmark count for a Waukesha County tax payment?

Yes, with limits. The treasurer follows Wis. Stat. 74.69(1): a mailed payment is timely if it is postmarked before midnight on the deadline, carries postage and reaches the treasurer within five business days. A postage meter date does not count as a postmark.

The county urges taxpayers to mail several days early, particularly from a community mailbox, and suggests asking a post office clerk to hand-cancel the envelope. Never mail cash. The office takes cashier's checks, money orders, personal checks or cash, in United States funds, and it may ask for guaranteed funds. Online, the fees are:

  • $1.50 for direct debit from a checking account
  • $3.95 for a debit card
  • 2.39 percent of the payment, with a $1.50 minimum, for a credit card

How do mortgage escrow payments work in Waukesha County?

The county accepts an escrow check made out to the county treasurer, the local treasurer or the deeded owner. If a check names you and a treasurer together, you cannot cash it yourself, because it must be applied to the tax.

When an escrow payment exceeds the bill, the county tells your local treasurer, who issues the refund. If the overpayment is on the second installment, the county sends a check within thirty days. These rules matter at a sale, since a lender that holds escrow may have paid part of the year already. Ask your servicer for a payment history, then ask the treasurer for a current statement, so the closing figures match.

How do I challenge an assessment in Waukesha County?

The value on your bill comes from your municipal assessor, and you object through your municipality's board of review. Under Wis. Stat. 70.47, the board meets once a year during the 45 days beginning on the fourth Monday of April. You need notice at least 48 hours before the first meeting and a written objection filed in its first two hours.

The glossary on the county site also explains why an assessed value may sit below market value. The Department of Revenue sets an average assessment ratio for each municipality, which compares assessed value to equalized value. Dividing your assessed value by that ratio gives an estimated fair market value, though the county says that figure is not used to calculate taxes.

Two credits reduce the final bill. The lottery and gaming credit under Wis. Stat. 79.10 applies to qualifying homeowners, and the school levy tax credit is funded by the state.

What does Waukesha County look like to a home seller?

Waukesha County covers 581 square miles west of Milwaukee, and its suburbs grew after Interstate 94 was built. The 2020 census counted 406,978 residents, which makes it the third most populous county in the state, and the 2025 estimate is 417,210. The county has 172,177 housing units, 4.4 percent of them vacant, and 75.2 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied.

The northwest corner is known as Lake Country, with Pewaukee, Delafield, Hartland, Merton, Nashotah, Chenequa, Oconomowoc, Summit and Lac La Belle. The cities are Brookfield, Delafield, Muskego, New Berlin, Oconomowoc, Pewaukee and Waukesha, which is the county seat. The 2020 median income was $88,985.

Your tax parcel number starts with two to four letters that identify the municipality, followed by six to ten digits. Have it ready when you call the treasurer about a payoff or a statement.

Frequently asked questions

When are Waukesha County property taxes due?

Most municipalities use January 31 and July 31. The City of Waukesha, City of New Berlin and Village of Sussex use January 31, March 31 and May 31 and collect those payments themselves.

How much interest does Waukesha County charge on delinquent taxes?

The charge is 1.5 percent per month on the unpaid balance, retroactive to February 1. The county describes this as 1 percent interest and a 0.5 percent penalty.

Where do I mail my Waukesha County tax payment?

Mail it to Waukesha County Treasurer, 515 W. Moreland Blvd., Room AC148, Waukesha, WI 53188 when the county is collecting. For communities that collect their own first installment, mail it to that municipality's treasurer.

What is a tax certificate in Waukesha County?

It is a lien the county issues every September 1 on properties with unpaid current-year taxes. The county must hold it for two years before foreclosure action can start, and paying the entire delinquency for that tax year voids the certificate.

Does Waukesha County take payments by card?

Yes, online. Direct debit costs $1.50, a debit card costs $3.95, and a credit card costs 2.39 percent with a $1.50 minimum. In person, the office takes cashier's checks, money orders, personal checks and cash.

Who collects property tax in Brown County, WI?

It depends on the municipality and the time of year. The Brown County Treasurer collects first-installment taxes for 12 municipalities only, and 13 others collect their own. After the first installment, unpaid and second-half taxes go to the county treasurer.

The Brown County Treasurer is at 305 E. Walnut Street, Room 160, Green Bay, WI 54301, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 23600, Green Bay, WI 54305. The phone number is 920-448-4074. Public hours are 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Thursday and 7:30 to 11:30 a.m. on Friday. The office keeps property tax records, collects taxes, and handles delinquent taxes and foreclosures.

The state rule sits in s. 74.11(6): payments made on or before January 31 go to the taxation district treasurer, and all other payments go to the county treasurer. Read your bill for the payee before you mail a check.

Which Brown County municipalities collect their own property taxes?

For the 2026 winter installment, the county's municipality page names 13 places that collect their own first-installment taxes. Payments for parcels in these places go to the local city, village or town and not to the county treasurer.

  • Cities: Green Bay (green bills) and De Pere (white bills).
  • Villages: Ashwaubenon, Bellevue, Denmark, Hobart, Howard, Pulaski and Suamico.
  • Towns: Holland, Ledgeview, Morrison and Rockland.

The county treasurer collects the winter installment for the rest, and those are the Brown bills:

  • Towns: Eaton, Glenmore, Green Bay, Humboldt, Lawrence, New Denmark, Pittsfield, Scott and Wrightstown.
  • Villages: Allouez, Greenleaf and Wrightstown.

Two places share the name Wrightstown, one a town and one a village, and Green Bay is both a city and a town. Match the full name on your bill before you pay.

When are Brown County property taxes due?

The county lists bills as mailed around December 10, a first installment due January 31 and a second due July 31. A taxpayer may also pay the whole bill by January 31 (s. 74.11(2)). State law requires the municipality to mail bills no later than the third Monday in December, which falls on December 21 this year (s. 74.09(5)).

Weekends move the practical deadlines. January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, and July 31, 2027 is a Saturday. The statute gives five working days after the due date, and when the due date falls on a weekend the window ends at the close of business on the first Friday of the next month.

What happens when a Brown County tax payment is late?

A missed first installment makes the entire unpaid balance delinquent as of February 1, and a missed second installment makes the unpaid balance delinquent as of August 1. Delinquent real property taxes are paid to the county treasurer along with interest and penalties charged from the preceding February 1 (s. 74.11(11)).

Failing to receive a bill does not change any of this. State law says a missing bill does not affect the validity of the tax or its collection (s. 74.09(6)). If your bill has not arrived by mid-December, call the treasurer or your municipal clerk. Ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure with interest if you are selling a parcel that is already delinquent.

How is a Brown County assessment set, and how do you appeal it?

A local assessor sets your assessed value, using the property's market value as of January 1. If you disagree, the formal appeal starts with your municipality's Board of Review under s. 70.47. The Department of Revenue's Guide for Property Owners, which the Brown County Treasurer posts on its forms page, walks through each step.

  • Attend the assessor's open book first. Any change to the roll after that requires the Board of Review or a court.
  • The Board of Review meets once a year inside a 45-day window that opens on the fourth Monday of April.
  • Give the board clerk oral or written notice of your intent to object at least 48 hours before the first meeting.
  • File a written, signed objection (form PA-115A) within the first two hours of that meeting, unless the board waives the deadline for good cause.
  • Bring evidence. The board presumes the assessor's value is correct until you show otherwise.

If the board rules against you, you can ask the circuit court to review the written record by certiorari within 90 days of the notice. A separate excessive assessment claim under s. 74.37 must be filed with the municipality by January 31 of the year the tax is payable, and you cannot file it after taking the board's decision to court.

What help is available with a Brown County tax bill?

The Department of Revenue guide lists several state programs that reduce or defer a bill, and the Brown County Treasurer handles one of them directly.

  • The lottery and gaming credit: forms LC-100 and LC-400 are the only ones returned to the Brown County Treasurer.
  • The homestead credit, an income-based credit for owners and renters, run by the Department of Revenue at 608-266-8641.
  • The property tax deferral loan for elderly homeowners, run by WHEDA at 800-755-7835. The loan becomes a lien and is repaid when you sell or move.
  • The first dollar credit, which appears on the bill as a reduction of taxes due.

If you are selling and know a deferral loan is in place, tell your title company early. It is repaid when ownership transfers.

What should a Brown County seller do about property tax at closing?

Ask your title company or closing agent for a tax figure before you sign, and split the current-year bill as your purchase contract directs. The 2026 winter bills go out in December, so a fall closing lands close to bill season.

  • Find the parcel number and the correct payee on the latest bill.
  • Ask the treasurer whether any prior-year balance is delinquent.
  • Confirm whether your municipality pays in two installments or in more.
  • Keep the receipt for any installment you have already paid and hand it to the closer.

The transfer itself is recorded at the register of deeds, and the seller owes the state transfer fee of $3 per $1,000 of value on a taxable sale.

What is Brown County like for property owners?

Brown County is Wisconsin's fourth most populous county and takes in the Green Bay metro area. Green Bay is the county seat, and De Pere is the other city. The county covers 616 square miles, of which 86 are water. Interstates 41 and 43 cross it, along with U.S. Highways 41 and 141.

School districts serving parts of the county include Green Bay Area, De Pere Unified, Ashwaubenon, Howard-Suamico, Pulaski Community, Denmark and Wrightstown Community. Your school district is one of the taxing jurisdictions on your bill, alongside the state, county, municipality and technical college district listed in the state guide.

Frequently asked questions

When are Brown County property taxes due?

The first installment or full payment is due January 31, and the second installment is due July 31. The county lists bills as mailed around December 10. Under s. 74.11, five working days of grace follow a due date, and a weekend due date pushes the cutoff to the first Friday of the next month.

Where do I pay property tax in Brown County?

It depends on your municipality. Thirteen cities, villages and towns collect their own first installment, including Green Bay and De Pere. The county treasurer collects for the other 12, such as Allouez and the Town of Scott. Check your bill. After January 31, payments go to the county treasurer.

Who sets my property tax assessment in Brown County?

A local assessor in your municipality sets it, based on market value as of January 1. To contest it, notify the Board of Review clerk 48 hours before the first meeting and file a written objection within the first two hours of that meeting.

What happens if I miss the January 31 payment in Brown County?

If the installment is not received within five working days after the due date, the whole unpaid balance becomes delinquent as of February 1. Delinquent taxes are paid to the county treasurer with interest and penalties charged from February 1.

Can I get help paying a Brown County property tax bill?

Possibly. The state offers an income-based homestead credit at 608-266-8641, a deferral loan for elderly homeowners through WHEDA at 800-755-7835, the lottery and gaming credit, and the first dollar credit. The county treasurer receives lottery and gaming forms LC-100 and LC-400.

Who sends and collects property tax bills in Racine County, Wisconsin?

In Racine County the local municipality sends the bill and collects the first payment, and the Racine County Treasurer collects what is paid afterward. Real estate tax bills are prepared and mailed in December. For every municipality except the City of Racine, two installments are allowed, January 31 and July 31, and the first installment goes to the local treasurer.

The County Treasurer's office is in the Racine County Courthouse, 1st floor at the north end, at 730 Wisconsin Avenue, and is open 8:00 am to 4:30 pm Monday through Friday. The phone is (262) 636-3239 and the email is rctreasurer@racinecounty.gov. A county page lists every municipal contact: the Towns of Burlington, Dover, Norway and Waterford, the Villages of Caledonia, Elmwood Park, Mount Pleasant, North Bay, Raymond, Rochester, Sturtevant, Union Grove, Waterford, Wind Point and Yorkville, and the Cities of Burlington and Racine.

What does Racine County look like for someone selling a house?

Racine County sits on Lake Michigan in southeastern Wisconsin between Milwaukee County to the north and Kenosha County to the south. It has 333 square miles of land and about 460 square miles of water, mostly lake. The 2020 census counted 197,727 residents, which made it the fifth most populous county in Wisconsin, and the 2025 estimate is 198,919.

Of the county's residents, 85.7 percent lived in urban areas, and 67.7 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied. The county started in 1836 as part of Wisconsin Territory, carved out of Milwaukee County, and it once reached the state's southern border before Kenosha County was created in 1850. Walworth and Waukesha counties border it to the west and northwest. That mix of lakeshore city, suburbs and farm towns means two houses in the same county can have different installment dates and different assessors.

Four offices cover most of what a seller needs: the municipal assessor, the local or county treasurer, the Register of Deeds, and the Board of Review clerk. The table lists the county contacts the county websites publish.

How can you pay Racine County property taxes?

You can pay the County Treasurer in person, by drop box, by mail or online. The office takes cash, checks and money orders at the counter. The drop box on the east side of the courthouse, facing Wisconsin Avenue, does not take cash. Mail goes to Racine County Treasurer, 730 Wisconsin Ave, Racine, WI 53403-1274.

  • Credit card or electronic check: call (800) 272-9829 or pay online through OfficialPayments.com with jurisdiction code 5835. Third-party fees apply.
  • Online search: the Ascent Land Records site shows the tax record, and you need the 15-digit parcel ID or tax key number to pay.
  • Notifications: the county lets owners sign up for text and email notices about tax parcels.

The county also publishes brochures on paying real estate taxes, taxpayer assistance resources, tax foreclosure and a glossary of tax terms, plus a how-to for looking up payment history.

What happens if a Racine County installment is late or short?

If any installment is late or short, all remaining taxes come due at once and interest and penalties begin on February 1. The rate is 1 percent interest per month plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty, 1.5 percent in all, under Wis. Stat. s. 74.47. The county says it has no authority to forgive any of it.

The statute adds a grace period. Under s. 74.11(7), the first installment counts as delinquent only if it is not received within five working days after January 31. For 2027, January 31 falls on a Sunday, so the period runs through the close of business on the first Friday in February. Still, the county's published position is that interest accrues from February 1 once an installment is missed, so pay by January 31 where you can.

For owners already behind, the County Treasurer's FAQ says taxpayers are encouraged to set up a regular payment plan and that monthly payments are accepted toward delinquent taxes. Ask the office for a payoff figure before you set a closing date.

How does tax foreclosure work in Racine County?

Racine County takes properties through tax foreclosure and then sells them at public sales run by the County Treasurer. The treasurer's page describes three types of sale: sealed bid, subsequent sealed bid and over-the-counter. A buyers' email list is available for notices of upcoming sales, and a separate Racine County Sheriff's Sale site covers sheriff's sales.

The county publishes a Tax Foreclosure FAQ brochure,. A homeowner who owes several years of tax and wants to sell has the best chance when the sale closes before foreclosure begins, so start by asking the treasurer which years are open and what the full payoff is.

How do you challenge a Racine County assessment?

You challenge an assessment before the municipal Board of Review, not the County Treasurer. Each town, village and city has its own board, and the clerk must publish notice at least 15 days before the first session, or 30 days in a revaluation year. The City of Racine posted a 2026 open book from June 8 to June 12 and a Board of Review on July 21, 2026, both of which have passed.

  • Give the board clerk written or oral notice at least 48 hours before the first meeting, unless you show good cause during the first two hours of that meeting.
  • File a written objection with the clerk in the first two hours of the first meeting.
  • Object to the total of land and buildings, because s. 70.47(7)(a) bars an objection to only one of them.
  • Testify under oath. The owner and the owner's witnesses are heard first.

Which Racine County tax credits can lower a bill?

Two credits come up most often on county pages. The lottery and gaming credit reduces the tax due on a qualified home, and owners now apply or remove it through the Department of Revenue's online portal. The county notes that late-claim applications must be submitted through the portal by the October 1 deadline.

The homestead credit is separate and is claimed when you file your Wisconsin income tax return. It is meant to soften the impact of property taxes and rent for people with lower incomes, and the county links the Department of Revenue fact sheet to check eligibility. The county also lists a veteran's property tax credit page.

What does the Racine County Register of Deeds handle?

The Register of Deeds is at 730 Wisconsin Avenue, with mailing at the same address, and takes real estate documents by drop-off, mail or electronic filing. Anyone who does not e-file is told to contact a title company or an electronic recording service provider. Public computers for document searching run from 8:30 am to 4:00 pm, first come, first served, and staff cannot help with searches.

State rules decide the cost. Recording a document is $30 under s. 59.43(2)(ag), and the real estate transfer fee is 30 cents for each $100 of value under s. 77.22. A transfer by will or survivorship is exempt, as are certain family transfers for nominal consideration.

How should a Racine County owner plan a sale with taxes due?

Work in this order: get the parcel record, call the treasurer who is collecting your installments, and confirm the full payoff, including any delinquent years and interest. A sale of a house in the City of Racine is handled differently from a sale in Mount Pleasant or Caledonia because the city uses four installments and the villages use two. After July 31, every payment, including City of Racine properties, goes to the County Treasurer.

Whatever kind of buyer you choose, the tax payoff, the deed and the transfer return still apply to the sale. Check every figure against the county's tax record before you accept an offer.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Racine County property taxes?

Pay your local municipality for the first installment, and pay the Racine County Treasurer at 730 Wisconsin Avenue for second installments and delinquent taxes. The City of Racine collects its own four installments through July 31.

What is the Racine County treasurer's phone number?

The Racine County Treasurer's phone is (262) 636-3239. The office is in the courthouse at 730 Wisconsin Avenue and is open 8:00 am to 4:30 pm Monday through Friday.

What interest do Racine County late taxes carry?

Delinquent taxes carry 1 percent interest and 0.5 percent penalty per month, 1.5 percent in total, under Wis. Stat. s. 74.47. The county says it cannot forgive them.

Can I pay Racine County taxes by card?

Yes. Call (800) 272-9829 or use OfficialPayments.com with jurisdiction code 5835. The county says third-party fees apply, and the drop box does not accept cash.

What does it cost to record a deed in Racine County?

Recording is $30 under Wis. Stat. s. 59.43(2)(ag), plus a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value under s. 77.22 unless an exemption applies. Call the Register of Deeds at (262) 636-3208 to confirm.

What makes Dane County property tax different from other Wisconsin counties?

Dane County is large, urban and split between many taxing bodies, and one city, Madison, collects its own current-year tax. The 2020 census counted 561,504 residents, which made Dane the second most populous county in Wisconsin after Milwaukee County, with nearly 10% of the state's people.

Madison is both the county seat and the state capital. The county covers 1,238 square miles, of which 1,197 are land. It was formed in 1836, organized in 1839, and named for Nathan Dane, a Massachusetts delegate who helped carve Wisconsin out of the Northwest Territory. Interstates 39, 90 and 94 cross it, along with U.S. 12, 14, 18, 51 and 151.

Housing is split between owners and renters. In 2020 there were 248,795 housing units and 238,417 households, and 56.3% of occupied units were owner-occupied against 43.7% rented. About 86.4% of residents lived in urban areas. The homeowner vacancy rate was 0.8% and the rental vacancy rate 3.9%.

The county's municipalities include:

  • Cities: Fitchburg, Madison, Middleton, Monona, Stoughton, Sun Prairie, Verona and Edgerton (mostly in Rock County).
  • Villages: Belleville, Black Earth, Blue Mounds, Brooklyn, Cambridge, Cottage Grove, Cross Plains, Dane, Deerfield, DeForest, Maple Bluff, Marshall, Mazomanie, McFarland, Mount Horeb, Oregon, Rockdale, Shorewood Hills, Waunakee and Windsor.
  • Many towns, from Albion and Berry to Westport and York, each with its own board and assessor.

When are Dane County property taxes due?

The first due date is January 31 and the final due date is July 31. Local municipalities mail bills on the third Monday of December, and Access Dane is updated with the new tax information the same day.

The county treasurer explains the cycle this way. Assessors set values as of January 1. Taxing districts set budgets in the fall. In December the tax is calculated from each assessment and the levies of the overlying districts. The calculation is assessment times mill rate for total taxes, minus the lottery credit and first dollar credit for net property taxes, plus special assessments and special charges for the bill itself.

January 1Municipal assessor determines valuesNone
Spring or summerNotice of Assessment, Open Book, then Board of ReviewLocal clerk and assessor
Third Monday of DecemberBills mailed by the local municipalityNone
January 31First due dateLocal municipality
July 31Final due dateDane County Treasurer, except City of Madison properties

Source: Dane County Treasurer, Property Tax 101.

The treasurer reports roughly how owners pay: about 30% pay in full in December, about 40% pay in full in January, and about 30% pay in installments. Madison differs because its bills have intermediate installments and the City Treasurer collects through the July 31 date. The Madison treasurer is at 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Room 107, phone (608) 266-4771.

What happens if a Dane County tax payment is late?

The whole bill comes due at once, and combined interest and penalty of 1.5% of the unpaid principal is added back to February 1. The charge accrues at the start of each month until principal, interest and penalty are paid in full.

The treasurer gives a worked example. An owner who is late with the final installment still owes the charge going back to February 1, so a payment in August carries seven months of it, or 10.5%. After that, each month adds another 1.5% to the outstanding principal.

Timeliness depends on the postmark, and the county warns that the Postal Service does not postmark mail the day it is dropped off. Practical options near a deadline:

  • Pay in person at the City-County Building, Room 114, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison. The office is open 8:00 to 4:00 Monday through Friday, excluding holidays, and has a drop box.
  • Pay by e-Check or credit card on the Treasurer's website.
  • Mail a check to Dane County Treasurer, PO Box 1299, Madison, WI 53701-1299, early enough to be postmarked on time.
  • If you pay through your bank, schedule it 7 to 10 business days ahead.

Delinquent taxes need a separate check to Dane County. A payment is not valid until it clears the bank, and a returned payment cancels the bills it covered.

How do you appeal a Dane County assessment?

Talk to your municipal assessor first, then go to the municipal Board of Review if you still disagree. The county treasurer notes that after the Board of Review it is normally too late to appeal the assessed value for that year.

The Notice of Assessment usually arrives in March or later. The Open Book period lets an owner discuss the numbers with the assessor, and the Board of Review hears formal appeals in a quasi-judicial setting. Wisconsin Statute 70.47 sets several firm rules:

  • The board meets within the 45-day period beginning the fourth Monday of April.
  • An owner must give notice at least 48 hours ahead and then file a written objection in the first two hours of the first meeting, unless the board waives the rule.
  • An owner who refused a reasonable certified-mail request from the assessor to view the exterior cannot appear before the board.
  • For property valued by the income method, the owner must send the assessor requested income and expense data no later than 7 days before the first meeting.
  • If the board waives the hearing, the owner has 60 days from the notice of waiver to start an excessive assessment action under Statute 74.37(3)(d).

The treasurer's page also links the Wisconsin Department of Revenue Guide for Property Owners and the Board of Review Member Guide. Each city, village and town runs its own board, so the local clerk tells you the date.

What if a Dane County property has already gone to tax deed?

A former owner can repurchase before the public auction, and the county sells what it acquired as is. Dane County does not sell tax deeds or tax liens. It sells properties it acquired through the tax deed process under Wisconsin Statute 75.35.

Auctions are usually held in October or November, and sometimes again in April or May. They use sealed bids. The bid due date is a Tuesday at 1:00 pm, and the bid opening is the next day at 10:00 am in the Treasurer's office. Each bid needs a form and a 10% earnest deposit. Payment is by cash or cashier's check only, and the buyer has ten days after the award notice to complete the purchase.

For former owners, repurchase is possible up to two weeks before the bid due date. If the parcel sells at auction, the county returns any net proceeds to the former owner. Occupants may still be living in parcels at the time of a fall auction, and the county lists occupant status with each parcel. The Treasurer's office asks that people not call for sale information, so read the Tax Deed Auction page first.

How do you sell a Dane County house with tax due?

Confirm the balance with the right treasurer, pay it at closing, and record the deed with the transfer return. Which treasurer you call depends on where the house is, because a Madison parcel and a parcel in Sun Prairie or Verona follow different collection routes.

  • Find the parcel number on the tax bill, or search Access Dane by address.
  • For Madison parcels, call the City of Madison Treasurer. For other parcels, ask the local municipal treasurer about tax due through January 31, and the Dane County Treasurer about the July 31 installment and any delinquent tax.
  • Record the deed at the Register of Deeds, phone (608) 266-4141, with the electronic Wisconsin Real Estate Transfer Return. The fee is 30 cents per $100 of value under Statute 77.22(1), charged to the grantor.
  • Update the mailing address after closing. Owner requests go in writing to Dane County Planning and Development, Property Listing, Room 116, or by email to property.listing@danecounty.gov.

When an owner has died, the county explains that the name comes off the record through a recorded Termination of Decedent's Interest for joint tenancy or survivorship marital property, or a Final Judgment for tenants in common. A transfer by will, descent or survivorship is exempt from the transfer fee under Statute 77.25(11).

January 31 is the first due date and July 31 is the final due date. The January payment goes to your local municipality, and the July payment goes to the Dane County Treasurer, except for City of Madison properties, which the City Treasurer collects through July 31.

What penalty applies to late Dane County property tax?

Combined interest and penalty of 1.5% of the unpaid principal per month, added back to February 1. Once an installment is missed, the full amount is due immediately, and an August payment carries seven months of the charge, which is 10.5%.

Where do I pay Dane County property tax in person?

At the Dane County Treasurer's office in the City-County Building, Room 114, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison. Hours are 8:00 to 4:00 Monday through Friday, excluding holidays, and a drop box is available.

Can I appeal my Dane County assessment after the Board of Review?

Usually not for that year. The county treasurer states that after the Board of Review it would normally be too late to appeal the assessed value. Talk to your assessor during the Open Book period and file with the board on time.

How do I change the billing address on a Dane County parcel?

Contact the municipal clerk or treasurer, or send a written request to Dane County Planning and Development, Property Listing, Room 116, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison, WI 53703. Email to property.listing@danecounty.gov is also accepted.

Who handles property tax in Outagamie County, Wisconsin?

Outagamie County property tax involves three layers: the municipal assessor, the county Property Listing Office, and the treasurer. The assessor sets the value in your city, village or town. The county's Property Listing Office keeps parcel ownership, legal descriptions, lottery credits and assessment records, and prepares the assessment roll, notices and tax bills. The Outagamie County Treasurer, at 320 S. Walnut Street in Appleton, receipts second installments and delinquent payments. The treasurer's phone number is (920) 832-5065.

The county says its tax collection follows Chapter 74 of the Wisconsin Statutes. If your mortgage lender holds an escrow account, the bill still goes to your mailing address, and the county says it is your job to work out with the lender how and when payments are made. Bills cannot be mailed to a mortgage loan or escrow agent.

When are Outagamie County property taxes due, and who gets the payment?

The first installment or the full payment is due to your local municipal treasurer by January 31. For 2025 taxes that date was January 31, 2026. The second installment, due July 31, and any delinquent payment can go to the county treasurer. Check the stubs at the top of your bill, which show the amount, the due date and where to send each payment.

The City of Appleton works differently. Current taxes for Appleton parcels are paid to the city, and the county points Appleton owners to the city website and to the Appleton phone number, (920) 832-6442. Other than Appleton, the county says all municipalities offer a two installment option.

State law supports the two installment schedule. Wis. Stat. 74.11 allows two equal installments, the first on or before January 31 and the second on or before July 31, and requires a parcel whose total tax is under $100 to be paid in full by January 31.

How do you pay the Outagamie County treasurer, and what does it cost?

You can pay online, by phone, by mail, in the deposit box or in person. The online system uses the nine digit parcel number, because the first three digits shown on a bill are for administrative use only. A property tax payment guide is posted by the county.

What happens if an Outagamie County tax payment is late?

A payment is not delinquent if it arrives within five working days of the January 31 or July 31 due date. The county's example is a July 31 due date with a grace date of August 7, and it accepts walk in payments through August 7 and mailed payments received by that date. The rule comes from Wis. Stat. 74.11(7) and 74.12(7).

After the grace period the consequences are firm:

  • If the first payment arrives after January 31, or the second installment after July 31, the taxes are delinquent and the full amount becomes due, whether you were paying in full or in installments.
  • Interest of one percent per month is charged on the unpaid balance starting February 1 under Wis. Stat. 74.47(1).
  • The county offers a monthly automatic deduction for delinquent real estate taxes, set up with a notarized payment agreement. Payments come out on the 10th or 25th of the month. Changes must reach the office by the 5th or 20th at (920) 832-5065.

The county also posts a delinquent tax report that anyone can download.

How does Appleton differ from the rest of Outagamie County?

Appleton is the county seat, and its tax collection is its own. The city accepts tax payments at City Hall, 100 N. Appleton St., at the first floor customer service desk, the drive-up window, the night deposit box, the lobby drop box, by mail to P.O. Box 2519, Appleton, WI 54912-2519, or online. Hours at the counter and drive-up are Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., except holidays.

Appleton offers four installments: January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. A late payment on any installment cancels the installment option and adds monthly interest from February 1, as state law requires. Outstanding balances on 2025 and earlier bills are delinquent and belong with the county treasurer. The delinquent payment goes to the treasurer of the county where the property is located, which can be Outagamie, Winnebago or Calumet: Outagamie (920) 832-5065, Calumet (920) 849-1457 or Winnebago (920) 232-3420.

How do you challenge a property assessment in Outagamie County?

Start with your local assessor. The county's Property Listing Office says that for assessment questions or disputes you should contact your local assessor to review your options, and it points to the Wisconsin Municipal Assessors List. You can look up your parcel on the county's Ascent Land Records site by parcel ID, address or name.

If you still disagree, the formal route is the board of review in your municipality. Wis. Stat. 70.47 requires an objector to give the board clerk written or oral notice at least 48 hours before the first meeting and to file a written objection in the first two hours of that meeting, unless the board waives the notice for good cause. Ask your municipal clerk for the meeting date and the form.

Prior-year assessment and tax rolls are on the county Open Data site. Current-year rolls are posted in January of the following year.

What tax credits can Outagamie County homeowners claim?

The lottery and gaming credit applies to a Wisconsin resident's primary residence as of January 1. It is not available on rentals, business property, vacant land or garages, and you may claim only one primary residence. The owner must apply; if the credit is missing from your bill, apply to the municipal treasurer by January 31 after you receive the bill, or file a late claim with the Department of Revenue by October 1.

Outagamie County's Property Listing Office also maintains lottery credits. Questions about a lottery credit on your parcel can go to the Property Listing Office, and the Real Property Lister is reachable at 920-832-5665.

What should you know when selling a house in Outagamie County?

First, find out who holds each payment. A seller in Appleton owes the city for current taxes and the county for anything delinquent. Elsewhere in the county, the first installment goes to the local treasurer, and the county can receipt the second.

  • Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure before closing, because the one percent monthly interest runs from February 1.
  • Confirm the owner and mailing address on the county record. Mailing address changes can be requested through the Ascent Land Records site and may take up to 24 hours to appear.
  • If your property has a lottery credit, the credit stays with the parcel, so ask your closing agent how the bill is divided under your contract.

What is Outagamie County like for homeowners?

Outagamie County is in the Fox Cities region in the northeast of Wisconsin. It was created in 1851, organized in 1852, and separated from Brown County, and it is named for the Meskwaki (Fox) people. Appleton is the county seat. The county covers 645 square miles, of which 638 are land, and it is governed by an elected county board and a county executive.

The Census Bureau estimated the county's population at 195,894 on July 1, 2025, up 2.7 percent from the 2020 base of 190,700. For 2020 to 2024 the owner-occupied rate was 71.5 percent, the median value of owner-occupied homes was $267,300, and median gross rent was $1,057. The county had 78,382 households and 82,646 housing units, and issued 1,022 building permits in 2025. Median household income was $85,069, and the mean commute was 20.5 minutes.

Pay the City of Appleton for current taxes, at City Hall, 100 N. Appleton St., by mail, or online. Appleton offers four installments on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. Delinquent balances go to the county treasurer.

What is the grace period for Outagamie County property tax?

State law gives five working days after January 31 or July 31. For July 31, the county shows August 7 as the last day. After that, the unpaid balance is delinquent and interest of one percent per month applies.

What interest does Outagamie County charge on late property tax?

Outagamie County cites Wis. Stat. 74.47(1) and charges one percent per month on the unpaid balance from February 1. Late payment on any installment makes the whole remaining tax due.

Who handles property tax in Rock County, Wisconsin?

Three layers touch a Rock County tax bill: the municipal assessor sets your value, the Real Property Description office keeps the parcel records, and the Rock County Treasurer collects most of the money. The Treasurer's office is in the Courthouse at 51 South Main Street, Janesville, WI 53545, open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone number is 608-757-5670.

The Real Property Description office serves every municipality in the county except the City of Beloit and the City of Janesville. That split matters when you move or sell. Address changes for Beloit and Janesville go to the Treasurer, while changes for the other 27 municipalities go to Real Property.

The county's Paying Property Taxes page says the tax notice mailed in December tells you where and when to pay. If no notice arrives by December 27, call the Treasurer or your local treasurer. You owe the tax whether or not a bill reaches you.

What does Rock County look like for someone selling a house?

Rock County covers 726 square miles in southern Wisconsin along the Illinois line, with Janesville as the county seat and largest city. The Rock River runs through the middle of the county and gave it its name. Territorial lawmakers created the county in 1836 and it was fully organized on February 19, 1839. Its cities are Beloit, Brodhead, Edgerton, Evansville, Janesville and Milton, and it borders Green, Dane, Jefferson and Walworth counties in Wisconsin and Boone and Winnebago counties in Illinois.

About 71% of homes are owner-occupied. The Census Bureau figures below come.

  • Population estimate, July 1, 2025: 166,472.
  • Housing units, July 1, 2025: 72,312.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $231,600.
  • Median household income: $75,673.
  • Median gross rent: $1,037.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, QuickFacts for Rock County.

When are Rock County property taxes due?

Most Rock County owners pay on January 31 and July 31, and Beloit owners get four dates. When your total for a parcel is more than $100, you can pay half by January 31 and the balance by July 31, or pay everything on January 31. A parcel at $100 or less is due in full on January 31, under s. 74.11(7) or 74.12 of the Wisconsin Statutes.

  • Everywhere except the City of Beloit: first payment or payment in full on January 31, second payment on July 31 to the County Treasurer only.
  • City of Beloit: four installments, January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31, every one paid to the County Treasurer.
  • Personal property taxes are due in full on January 31.

In December and January, four towns collect the first payment locally. After January 31, the County Treasurer collects real estate taxes for every municipality, and the county tells owners not to send payments to a local treasurer after that date.

What happens if a Rock County tax payment is late?

A missed installment cancels the installment option, and the whole unpaid balance becomes delinquent. Delinquent taxes carry interest of 1.5% per month from February 1 until paid, and a fraction of a month counts as a full month. The county describes this as 18% a year under s. 74.11(7) or 74.12.

The Treasurer honors United States Postal Service postmarks and does not accept metered marks. If you mail a check on the last day, ask the post office to hand cancel the envelope. Checks go to the Rock County Treasurer, and cash is taken in person only.

  • Card and e-check payments run through GovTech Services: 2.29% for credit, $3.95 for debit, $1.00 for an e-check.
  • Phone payments use 1-855-912-7625, and the county says to allow 5 to 10 business days for electronic payments to arrive.
  • Owners whose first payment goes to one of the four towns cannot use GovTech for that payment.
  • A Courthouse drop box sits before security, and a second one is beside the Treasurer's door on the second floor.

If your lender pays from escrow, you still receive the notice. Confirm with the lender when and how it pays, and ask for the lender's tax escrow option notice if you want a different payment date.

How do I challenge my Rock County assessment?

Start with the valuation notice from your assessor and follow the protest steps printed on it. The county tells owners that the tax is built from assessed value, and that you should also attend budget meetings for your school district, technical college, county and municipality. Your assessor's rules, not the Treasurer's, decide the details, so ask your town, village or city clerk for the dates.

The statewide steps come from the Department of Revenue's Guide for Property Owners and s. 70.47.

  • Talk to the assessor at open book. Changes after open book need a formal process.
  • The Board of Review meets during the 45 days that begin on the fourth Monday in April, at least seven days after open book.
  • Give the clerk notice of your objection at least 48 hours before the first meeting, and file a signed objection form (PA-115A) in the first two hours of that meeting. A good-cause waiver is possible.
  • You object to the total value of land and buildings together, and the board presumes the assessor is right until you show otherwise.
  • A board ruling can be appealed to the Department of Revenue under s. 70.85 within 20 days of delivery (a $100 fee applies), or to circuit court under s. 70.47(13) within 90 days.
  • An excessive assessment claim under s. 74.37 needs a prior Board of Review appeal and must reach the municipality by January 31 of the year the tax is payable.

Which credits and help programs does Rock County point owners to?

The Treasurer's page lists state credits and a loan program rather than a county exemption. Each is run by the agency named, so contact that agency, not the county, to apply.

  • Wisconsin Department of Revenue income tax credits: Homestead Credit, Farmland Tax Relief Credit and School Property Tax Credit.
  • Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection: Farmland Preservation Credit.
  • WHEDA property tax deferral loans for the elderly, 1-800-755-7835.
  • Property tax credits shown on the bill: Lottery and Gaming Credit, First Dollar Credit and School Levy Tax Credit.

Eligibility rules and filing dates change. Ask the agency for the current form before you rely on any credit when you budget for a payoff.

What should a Rock County seller do about property tax before closing?

Get the current balance in writing and give it to the title company. Ask the Rock County Treasurer for the amount due on your parcel, including any interest, so the closing statement matches the county's records. If you are behind, the 1.5% monthly interest keeps running until the county is paid.

Name changes follow recorded deeds. The county says its records reflect the most recently recorded document, so the new owner's name appears on later bills only after the deed is recorded with the Register of Deeds. The office takes walk-in visitors and has a drop box in the Courthouse lobby.

Wisconsin sellers of one to four unit homes must also hand the buyer a completed real estate condition report within 10 days after the contract is accepted. A buyer who does not receive it may rescind within two business days after that period ends (s. 709.02). Each municipality mails bills by mid-December. According to the county treasurer FAQ, you should call your local treasurer if no bill arrives by December 20. A missing bill does not excuse a late payment or the interest that follows.

When are Walworth County property taxes due and where do I pay?

If you want a receipt for a mailed payment, enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope, and know that the receipt is not valid until the payment clears the banks. The county warns that a property delinquent for two or more years is subject to foreclosure. Walworth County uses the in rem tax foreclosure procedure, which the county treasurer oversees. Under Wis. Stat. 75.521, the treasurer can file a list of liens with the circuit court two years after the tax certificate date. Anyone with an interest in a listed parcel may redeem by paying the sums in the list with interest and the county's costs, or may file a verified answer within 30 days after the last redemption date in the published notice. Lake Geneva, Alpine Valley Resort and Alpine Valley Music Theatre draw visitors, and the county ranked sixth in the state for tourism impact, close to $1 billion in 2023. The cities are Burlington, Delavan, Elkhorn, Lake Geneva and Whitewater, and the villages include Bloomfield, Darien, East Troy, Fontana-on-Geneva Lake, Genoa City, Mukwonago, Sharon, Walworth and Williams Bay.

Several of these places cross county lines. Burlington sits mostly in Racine County, Whitewater partly in Jefferson County, Genoa City partly in Kenosha County and Mukwonago mostly in Waukesha County. Check the county printed on your tax bill before you decide which treasurer to call.

Yes. Property that is delinquent for two or more years is subject to foreclosure, and the county treasurer runs the in rem procedure. Interested parties can redeem by paying what is owed plus costs before the redemption deadline in the published notice.

Who handles questions about my Walworth County assessment?

Your local assessor does, and you can then go to your municipal board of review. The county treasurer does not set or change assessed values.

Assessment is a separate job done at the municipal level, so ask your town, village or city clerk who your assessor is. The county's Real Property Listing office (715-386-4680) answers questions about how an owner's name and parcel appear on the tax bill.

The county mails one tax statement per parcel each year to the owner of record. If the deed changes hands after the bills are printed, the county does not mail a new statement, so a buyer may need to ask the treasurer or the local clerk for a copy of the bill.

When are St. Croix County property taxes due?

The first installment, or the full payment, is due January 31, and the second installment is due July 31. Wisconsin bills property tax in arrears, so a bill issued in December 2026 pays for 2026 and is due starting January 31, 2027.

The county says bills arrive in mid-December. Under Wis. Stat. 74.11, a bill under $100 must be paid in full by January 31, and a first installment that is not received within five working days of January 31 makes the whole unpaid balance delinquent on February 1. January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, so the statute moves the end of that five-working-day period to the close of business on Friday, February 5. How do you appeal a St. Croix County assessment?

You appeal to your municipality's board of review, not to the county. Under Wis. Stat. 70.47, the board meets once a year during the 45-day period that begins on the fourth Monday of April.

The credit does not apply to rentals, vacant land or garages. When a qualifying house sells, the credit goes with the property, so it should be counted when the buyer and seller prorate taxes. St. Croix County, with Hudson as its seat, sits on the Minnesota border and is part of the Minneapolis-St. Paul metropolitan area. No. The county says a change of ownership recorded after the bills are printed does not trigger a new statement. The bill goes to the owner on record, so a buyer should ask the treasurer for a copy.

What is Milwaukee County like for someone selling a house with taxes due?

Milwaukee County is the most populous and most densely populated county in Wisconsin. The 2020 census counted 939,489 residents, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 924,216, a decline of 1.6 percent. About 241 square miles are land, and another 948 square miles are water, for 1,189 square miles in all. The city of Milwaukee is the county seat. The state's 2026 Guide for Property Owners says an owner who pays in installments owes the first payment by January 31 and the second by July 31, unless the local government set a different schedule. How do I pay a City of Milwaukee property tax bill?

The City Treasurer accepts payment by mail, in a drop box, by phone or online. The office is at City Hall, Room 103, 200 East Wells Street, Milwaukee, WI 53202, and the customer service line is 414-286-2240. Cash is not accepted.

  • Mail a check with the return envelope from your bill, mailing early because the Postal Service moved its postmarking to regional centers on December 24, 2025.

How do I pay delinquent taxes to the Milwaukee County Treasurer?

The office collects back taxes through payments, Wisconsin Tax Refund Intercept (TRIP), foreclosure or a lawsuit against the individual. How do I challenge a Milwaukee County property assessment?

A property owner can ask the board to waive the hearing and go straight to circuit court, but a granted waiver ends the right to claim an excessive assessment or appeal to the Department of Revenue. A court action under section 70.47(13) must begin within 90 days of the waiver notice.

Disputes over exemptions skip the Board of Review. An owner contesting exempt status files a claim of unlawful tax with the municipality by January 31 of the year the tax is payable, under section 74.35. Your city or village clerk can tell you the Board of Review dates.

If taxes stay unpaid, Milwaukee County uses the in rem foreclosure process, in which title to a delinquent property can be transferred under Wisconsin law. After the sale, the new owner should record the change with the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds. Installment payers owe the first half by January 31 and the second half by July 31 unless the local government set a different schedule. A missed first installment makes the whole balance delinquent as of February 1 once five working days have passed.

Where does Chippewa County sit, and what does that mean for home sellers?

Chippewa County lies in west-central Wisconsin and is part of the Eau Claire metropolitan area. The county seat and largest city is Chippewa Falls, and the 2020 census counted 66,297 residents, with a 2025 estimate of 67,614.

The county covers 1,041 square miles, of which 1,008 are land and 33 are water. The Chippewa River runs through the middle of the county, past Lake Wissota and out between Chippewa Falls and Eau Claire. The highest ground is the Flambeau Ridge west of Holcombe. A band of hills left by the last glacier crosses the county, and the Ice Age Trail follows it. South of those hills, much of the land is rolling till plain with fertile ground along the streams.

Housing is mostly owner-occupied. The 2020 census listed 28,688 housing units, of which 8.4% were vacant, and among occupied homes 73.7% were owned and 26.3% rented. About 37.5% of residents lived in urban areas and 62.5% in rural ones, so a sale here can mean a lot in Chippewa Falls or a farmhouse on acreage, and the tax questions differ for each.

Communities that bill property tax inside the county include:

  • Cities: Bloomer, Chippewa Falls, Cornell, Stanley (partly in Clark County) and the part of Eau Claire that lies in Chippewa County.
  • Villages: Boyd, Cadott, Lake Hallie and New Auburn (partly in Barron County).
  • Unincorporated places such as Holcombe, Jim Falls and Lake Wissota.

Who collects property tax in Chippewa County?

Your local treasurer collects first, and the Chippewa County Treasurer collects what is left over later. All payments made in December and January on the current year tax go to the town, village or city treasurer.

The county treasurer's office describes its work as receiving and depositing money, collecting all postponed and delinquent real estate taxes, making tax settlements with the taxing districts, maintaining the lottery credit file and property listing, producing the assessment and tax rolls, printing the tax bills, handling tax deeds, and answering questions about property values, legal descriptions and tax information. It also holds unclaimed funds.

The treasurer's web pages gather several tools for owners:

  • Current mill rates and credits.
  • Lottery credit FAQs and forms.
  • A Property Owners Guide in PDF form.
  • An assessor list and a list of local treasurer addresses and phone numbers.
  • Online tax lookup and payment through the county's public portal.

Ask the county treasurer for the current mill rates and credits before estimating a bill, because the treasurer's page publishes them each year.

When are Chippewa County property taxes due, and what is the penalty?

The first installment, or the whole bill, is due January 31, and the second installment is due July 31. Missing the first date makes the entire unpaid balance delinquent.

How does a Chippewa County Board of Review appeal work?

You file an objection with the Board of Review of your own town, village or city, and the board decides after a hearing. Wisconsin Statute 70.47 governs the process, so the rules are the same in every Wisconsin municipality, though the dates are set locally.

The board meets once a year within a 45-day window that starts on the fourth Monday of April, and the clerk publishes notice at least 15 days beforehand. Here is what an owner needs to prepare:

  • Written or oral notice to the clerk at least 48 hours before the first meeting that you intend to object.
  • A written objection filed within the first two hours of that meeting, on a form the board may require.
  • Your own opinion of value for the land and for the improvements, plus the information behind it.
  • Willingness to testify under oath. The board may allow a hearing by phone or sworn written statements.

The burden sits with the owner. The board presumes the assessor's valuation is correct, and an owner has to show it is wrong with evidence. Votes are by roll call, and a tie sustains the assessment. An owner who refuses a reasonable written request by certified mail from the assessor to view the exterior of the property can lose the right to appear. Ask your municipal clerk for the meeting date, since the county does not set it.

What shapes housing demand in Chippewa County?

Jobs in Chippewa Falls and the wider Eau Claire area drive most of it. The county's largest employers, as Wikipedia lists them, include TTM Advanced Circuits, Chippewa Falls Public Schools, Saint Joseph's Hospital, the Wisconsin Department of Corrections, Walmart, Mason Companies, Chippewa County itself, Mayo Health System and Cooperative Educational Service Agency 10.

Population has grown in each census since 1990. It went from 52,360 in 1990 to 55,195 in 2000, 62,415 in 2010 and 66,297 in 2020. Chippewa Valley Regional Airport and Eau Claire Transit connect the county to the larger Eau Claire area, and Chippewa Falls has a small intermodal terminal on the Canadian National line.

For a seller, that mix means a steady local market near the cities and a thinner one on large rural parcels. On any parcel, confirm which town, village or city treasurer takes the January payment.

How do you sell a Chippewa County house with property tax unpaid?

Find the balance, decide who pays what at closing, and record the deed with the transfer return. A sale can close with taxes owed as long as the payoff is arranged.

  • Phone the Chippewa County Treasurer and ask for the parcel's balance, including interest at the rate the county charges on delinquent accounts.
  • Find out whether the first installment went to the local treasurer and whether the July 31 installment is still open.
  • Ask the closing agent to pay the tax from the seller's proceeds.
  • Expect the Register of Deeds to collect the state transfer fee when the deed is recorded. Wisconsin Statute 77.22 sets it at 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction, charged to the grantor.

Inherited homes often move this way. A conveyance by will, descent or survivorship is exempt from the transfer fee under Statute 77.25(11), and a transfer between parent and child for little or no consideration is exempt under 77.25(8). The return still shows the value and the exemption number.

A house in Chippewa Falls, Bloomer or Lake Hallie follows the same steps as a farm near Cadott or Cornell. Only the municipality's treasurer changes.

January 31 is the due date for the full bill or the first installment, and July 31 is the due date for the second installment. Pay the first to your local treasurer. Pay the second to the Chippewa County Treasurer.

The county page states interest of 1% per month. It begins February 1 on the unpaid balance after a missed first installment, and a missed July 31 payment is charged 1% per month retroactive to February 1.

You pay it to the Chippewa County Treasurer. The county states that all delinquent taxes are paid there, not to the local treasurer.

No. Bills under $100 must be paid in full by January 31 to the local treasurer.

Who sets my property value in Chippewa County?

Your municipality's assessor sets it, and the municipal Board of Review hears appeals each spring. The county treasurer's site carries an assessor list, so call the treasurer if you cannot tell who assesses your parcel.

Sauk County is a mid-sized rural county of 849 square miles whose seat and largest city is Baraboo. It was created in 1840 and organized in 1844. Any unpaid amount has to be settled at or before closing, and the County Treasurer can give you the balance. Share that figure with the title company so it comes out of the proceeds. Who handles property tax in Calumet County?

Two layers handle it. Each town, village and city in Calumet County contracts its own assessor and runs its own treasurer, while the Calumet County Treasurer in Chilton takes care of the county side of the work.

The county treasurer is Mike Schlaak. The office is at 206 Court Street in Chilton, keeps hours Monday through Friday from 8 am to 4:30 pm, and answers at (920) 849-1457. According to the county, the treasurer receives all county delinquent and postponed real estate taxes, takes the first installment for the City of New Holstein, settles the tax rolls with the towns, villages, cities and school districts, sends the delinquent notices and processes every property that becomes eligible for tax foreclosure.

A second job, the Real Property Lister, sits in the same office. Each time a property changes owners, a Transfer Form is recorded at the Register of Deeds. The recorded form then goes to the treasurer's office so the billing information on the parcel can change. The lister also builds the tax rolls for the municipal assessors, and the values from each assessor usually arrive between late February and late May.

What should a Calumet County home seller know about the county?

Calumet County is small, farm-heavy and bordered by water. It covers 397 square miles, but 79 of those are water, mostly Lake Winnebago along the western boundary. By land area it is the fifth-smallest county in Wisconsin.

Chilton is the county seat, and the county was organized in 1850. The 2020 census counted 52,442 residents, and the 2025 Census estimate is 53,982. The county sits inside the Appleton metropolitan area, and pieces of Appleton, Kaukauna and Menasha reach into its northwest corner. The southern end is known as the Holyland, settled in the 1840s by emigrants from the Schleswig-Holstein region of Germany. Earlier, in the 1830s, the Brothertown, Oneida and Stockbridge-Munsee peoples were relocated to the southwest part of the county.

Getting around is simple. No interstate crosses the county. U.S. 10 runs east to west along the northern edge, U.S. 151 runs near the western edge, Wisconsin 55 follows the western side, and Wisconsin 32/57 passes through the middle. The Niagara Escarpment runs north to south several miles east of Lake Winnebago, and glaciers shaped the rolling ground around it.

Farmland matters for taxes here. The county's tax bill guide explains that agricultural land is assessed on its ability to produce, so a farm parcel can show a zero estimated market value on the bill. A seller with acreage should read the bill closely before talking numbers with a buyer.

When are Calumet County property taxes due?

Full payment or the first installment is due January 31, and the second installment is due July 31. Local treasurers mail the real and personal property tax bills in early to mid December.

A bill over $100 can be split. The first half goes to the local treasurer by January 31, and the second half goes to the Calumet County Treasurer by July 31. The county's tax bill guide adds that the first installment must be paid in full and on time to keep the installment option. Personal property tax is paid to the local treasurer in full by January 31, unless the bill shows an installment option.

Mail needs a postmark on or before the due date, and a hand-delivered payment must reach the correct treasurer by that date. The county bill insert also says a payment received within five business days after the due date can still count as timely, a rule tied to Wisconsin Statute 74.69. Treat that as a safety net and pay early.

Which taxing districts appear on a Calumet County tax bill?

Up to five main districts can appear: the State of Wisconsin, Calumet County, a technical college, the municipality and a school district. Some parcels also sit inside a special district for a lake, sewer or fire protection, and that district takes a share too.

The county lists these local districts:

  • Towns: Brillion, Brothertown, Charlestown, Chilton, New Holstein, Rantoul, Stockbridge and Woodville.
  • Villages: Harrison, Hilbert, Potter, Sherwood and Stockbridge.
  • Cities: Brillion, Chilton and New Holstein, plus the Calumet County portions of Appleton, Kaukauna, Menasha and Kiel.
  • Technical colleges: Fox Valley, Moraine Park and Lakeshore.
  • School districts: Appleton, Brillion, Chilton, Hilbert, Kaukauna, Kiel, Kimberly, Menasha, New Holstein, Stockbridge and Wrightstown.

Two credits can reduce the bill. The first dollar credit goes to a property with a structure, whatever its use or value. The lottery and gaming credit goes to a property used as the owner's primary residence. The bill also shows an average assessment ratio for the municipality, which compares assessed values with the state's estimate of fair market value drawn from arm's length sales.

How do you appeal a Calumet County assessment?

Your municipality's Board of Review hears the appeal. Calumet County assessors work for the individual town, village or city, so the board that hears your case sits in the place where the house stands.

Wisconsin Statute 70.47 sets the steps. The board meets during a 45-day window that begins on the fourth Monday of April, and the clerk must publish notice at least 15 days ahead (30 days in a year with a revaluation). The deadlines are tight:

  • Tell the board clerk, in writing or by phone, at least 48 hours before the first meeting that you plan to object.
  • File the written objection during the first two hours of that first meeting. The board can waive these steps for good cause or extraordinary circumstances.
  • Object to the combined value of land and improvements. An owner cannot challenge only the land or only the building.
  • State your own estimate of value in writing, with the information behind it, and be ready to testify under oath.

The board presumes the assessor's value is correct, and a tie vote leaves the assessment in place. Statute 70.47 also points to a claim for excessive assessment under Statute 74.37 for owners who go beyond the board. Ask the municipal clerk for the date of the next board meeting, because it changes each year.

What happens to a Calumet County house when taxes go unpaid?

The tax becomes delinquent, interest and penalty grow, and the county can eventually foreclose. Delinquent real property taxes are paid to the Calumet County Treasurer, while delinquent personal property taxes are paid to the local treasurer.

The charge is 1.5% per month from February 1, and notices go out in February and August. When a parcel reaches the stage where it is eligible for tax foreclosure, the treasurer processes it. The treasurer's page announced a property tax auction ending December 7, 2026 at 10:00 am, so an owner with a delinquent parcel should call the office before that date to learn where the parcel stands.

An owner who plans to sell has more options before foreclosure than after it. Getting a payoff figure early and settling the account at closing keeps the sale moving.

How do you sell a Calumet County house with tax due?

Get the exact balance from the treasurer, then settle it through closing. The balance depends on which installment has been paid, so the figure on last December's bill is only a starting point.

  • Call the Calumet County Treasurer at (920) 849-1457 and ask what is owed on the parcel, including any interest and penalty.
  • Ask whether the first installment went to the local treasurer and whether the second installment is still open for July 31.
  • Give the closing agent the parcel details so unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds.
  • Record the deed at the Register of Deeds with the electronic transfer return. Wisconsin charges the grantor a fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction under Statute 77.22(1), and the register collects it at recording.
  • After recording, the Real Property Lister updates the billing name and address on the parcel.

A house with a delinquent balance can still sell. The paperwork just needs the tax figure early, so the buyer's title work and the payoff line up.

When are Calumet County property taxes due?

Taxes are due January 31 for full payment or the first installment, and July 31 for the second installment. The first goes to your local treasurer. The second goes to the Calumet County Treasurer in Chilton.

What interest does Calumet County charge on late property tax?

The county states a rate of 1.5% per month, counted from February 1. The charge applies to a late first installment or a late second installment, and the unpaid tax is treated as delinquent.

Who sets the value of my Calumet County home?

A municipal assessor sets it. Each town, village and city contracts its own assessor, who sends values to the county's Real Property Lister, typically between late February and late May. The Wisconsin Department of Revenue separately estimates fair market value from arm's length sales for the bill.

Can I pay my Calumet County tax bill in two parts?

Yes, if the bill is over $100. Pay the first installment on time to your local treasurer by January 31 to keep the option, then pay the second to the county treasurer by July 31. Miss the first date and the installment option is lost.

Which credits lower a Calumet County tax bill?

The first dollar credit and the lottery and gaming credit. The first dollar credit applies to any property with a structure. The lottery and gaming credit applies to property used as the owner's primary residence.

How does a board of review hearing work in Washington County?

  • Rental units

  • Business property

A person temporarily away for about six months or less, for example in a hospital, still has the home they return to as their residence.

Washington County is the fifth-smallest county in Wisconsin by area, at 436 square miles, and it sits in the Milwaukee metro area north of Waukesha County. West Bend is the county seat. Hartford is the other city of any size, and the villages include Germantown, Jackson, Kewaskum, Newburg, Richfield and Slinger. Schools include Germantown, Kewaskum, Slinger and Hartford Union high schools, and the county contains part of the Kettle Moraine State Forest.

Commuting is a point buyers raise. The county ended its Commuter Express service at the end of 2023, so there is no public transit link from Washington County to the rest of the Milwaukee metro area, though shared ride taxi service remains. A Wisconsin resident who owns a home and uses it as a primary residence on January 1 of the levy year qualifies. You must apply, and rentals, vacant land and garages do not qualify.

Give notice to your municipal board of review at least 48 hours before its first meeting and file a written objection in the first two hours of that meeting. The board meets during a 45-day window that begins on the fourth Monday of April.

What should a seller know about Barron County before dealing with property tax?

The county was created in 1859 as Dallas County, renamed Barron County in 1869 and organized in 1874.

The 2020 census listed 23,779 housing units, of which 17.4 percent were vacant, and 73.2 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied. The incorporated places are the cities of Barron, Chetek, Cumberland and Rice Lake and the villages of Almena, Cameron, Dallas, Haugen, New Auburn, Prairie Farm and Turtle Lake. Those places and the surrounding towns each have a treasurer who collects first-installment payments.

Which Barron County office handles my property tax?

The Barron County Treasurer and Real Property Lister is the county office to know. It sits at 335 E Monroe Ave, Room 2412, Barron, WI 54812-1478, is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, and answers at 715-537-6280. The Real Property Lister side keeps the parcel descriptions that feed the assessment and tax roll, pulling together records from the Register of Deeds, surveying, zoning and mapping, the assessor and the treasurer. Wisconsin sets the dates by statute. Under Wis. Stat. 74.11, real property tax is paid in full or in two equal installments, with the first due January 31 and the second July 31. Interest and penalty run back to February 1. The county lists 10.5 percent as the August charge on 2025 taxes still unpaid after the July 31, 2026 installment date, and notes that 2025 taxes are due in 2026 because taxes follow the prior year's assessment.

Under state law, a late first installment makes the whole unpaid balance delinquent as of February 1. Mail timing deserves attention:

  • A mailed check must be postmarked on or before the due date.
  • The county warns that local mail is often postmarked in Saint Paul, Minnesota, sometimes days later, so take the envelope to the local post office and ask for a hand stamp.
  • Envelopes that arrive with no postmark cannot be treated as timely.

Counties and municipalities can sue an owner to recover delinquent taxes that came due during that owner's period of ownership, normally after the county board or governing body approves, and only up to the amount owed plus interest and penalties, under chapter 74.

Stat. 77.22, and its exemption list in section 77.25 cover conveyances by will or descent, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the lender and transfers between a parent and child for little or no payment.
