Which office handles property tax in La Crosse County?

The La Crosse County Treasurer handles it after January 31, and your municipal treasurer takes the first payment. The County Treasurer's office is in the Administration Center at 212 6th Street North, La Crosse, WI 54601. Phone is (608) 785-9711, email is treasurer@lacrossecounty.org, and hours are 8:00 am to 4:30 pm on weekdays.

The state rule is in Wis. Stat. 74.11(6): payments made on or before January 31 go to the taxation district treasurer, and all other payments go to the county treasurer. The county's guidance for first installment amounts is to ask the treasurer of your city, village or town. After the first deadline, call the county office.

Assessments are a separate function. The county's Zoning and Land Information office keeps the parcel records and the public property portal (608-785-9722). Each municipality's assessor sets the values. The county's FAQ says its staff must maintain the values the municipal assessor established and cannot change them, so a disagreement goes to the assessor first.

When are La Crosse County property taxes due?

You can pay the whole bill by January 31, or pay in two installments, the first by January 31 and the second by July 31. The county's sample tax bill sheet lists those two options, and Wis. Stat. 74.11(2) provides for two installments unless the total real property tax on a parcel is under $100, in which case it is due in full by January 31. A municipality can adopt a three-installment ordinance under 74.12, so ask your local treasurer if your bill shows more than two payment slips.

Both 2027 dates fall on a weekend. January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, so the five-working-day window runs to Friday, February 5, 2027 (74.11(7)(b)). July 31, 2027 is a Saturday, and the window runs to Friday, August 6, 2027 (74.11(8)(b)). Mailing early is still the safer choice. Under 74.69(1), a postmarked payment counts as timely if it reaches the proper official within five business days after the due date.

What does a late payment cost in La Crosse County?

It costs 1.5 percent a month on the unpaid balance, and you lose the installment option. The 1 percent comes from Wis. Stat. 74.47(1). La Crosse County Ordinance 4.05 adds the 0.5 percent penalty allowed under 74.47(2). Both are counted per month or fraction of a month, back to February 1.

Several rules decide how a partial payment is handled:

  • Missing the first installment by the deadline makes the entire remaining balance delinquent as of February 1 (74.11(7)).
  • Delinquent real property tax, with its interest and penalty, is paid to the county treasurer (74.11(11)).
  • A short payment is applied in a set order. The association's FAQ, citing 74.12(11)(a), lists the order: personal property taxes first, then delinquent utility charges, special charges, special assessments and special taxes, with real property tax last.
  • Treasurers cannot waive interest for hardship. The WI County Treasurers Association says the only exceptions are a severe postal error and active military deployment of 90 days or more.

If you cannot cover an installment, pay as much as you can by the deadline and keep paying monthly. The association's FAQ gives an example in which a $500 payment covers a $200 special charge first, so only $300 reaches the tax.

What is on a La Crosse County tax bill?

The bill shows four main taxing jurisdictions: the county, the school district, the local technical college and your municipality. Parcels inside a lake district or sanitary district also carry that district's share. The county's sample bill sheet explains each box. The net assessed value rate is the combined mill rate of every jurisdiction, applied to your total assessed value, and the product is your tax before the lottery credit.

The bill also gives an estimated fair market value, which the Department of Revenue calculates from arm's-length sales in the past year. That is not an appraisal and it is not what the house will sell for. The average assessment ratio compares your municipality's assessed values with market value. Land and improvements are taxed at the same rate even when their values differ, and any recently passed referenda must be listed on the bill under state law.

If you do not get a bill by December 21, call your municipal treasurer. A missing bill does not stop interest from running (74.09(6)).

How do I appeal a La Crosse County assessment?

Start with the assessor for your municipality, then use the municipal Board of Review. For the City of La Crosse, the Assessor's Office is at 608-789-7525 (assessor@cityoflacrosse.org) and the City Clerk's Office at 608-789-7510 handles Board of Review filings. The city says most questions are answered in an informal review. If you still disagree, file written or oral notice of intent with the city clerk at least 48 hours before the board opens, then file an approved objection form before or within the first two hours of the first meeting.

The city describes its Board of Review as a quasi-judicial body of five appointed residents that works like a court. Its job is to weigh the facts offered at the hearing, and the owner must show that the property is assessed unfairly compared with the general level of assessment in the district. State law sets the calendar: the board meets during the 45 days that begin on the fourth Monday of April (70.47(1)).

The City of La Crosse did an interim revaluation for 2026. Open book ran April 29 to May 6, 2026, and the first Board of Review meeting was May 14, 2026, so the 2026 window has closed. After the board decides, court review is by certiorari, filed within 90 days after the notice of decision (70.47(13)). Outside the city, ask the village or town clerk for the schedule.

What do La Crosse County parcel records mean for a seller?

The names on a tax bill come from recorded documents at the Register of Deeds, so ownership problems show up on the bill first. The county's Real Property FAQ gives several practical rules:

  • After a divorce, the former spouse's name stays on bills and notices until a recorded document, such as a quit claim deed or divorce judgment, changes title.
  • After a death, a joint tenancy or survivorship marital property parcel can be cleared by filing a Termination of Decedent's Interest form with the Register of Deeds. Other titles may need an attorney and probate.
  • A parcel split during the year is billed as a whole to the owner at the time of the split, and the new parcels are assessed and taxed the next year. Assessments reflect the property as it stood on January 1.
  • Mailing address changes go through the municipal treasurer or the county office.
  • The public portal searches by owner name, address, parcel number or tax bill number, and the parcel format is ##-#####-### with zeros filled in.

When a deed is delivered, Wis. Stat. 74.15 sets a default tax split if the contract says nothing: the seller owes the buyer a monthly share equal to one-twelfth of last year's tax, covering every month before the deed plus the sale month if the deed falls after the 15th. For a payoff on delinquent tax, call the County Treasurer.

Are there property tax credits for La Crosse County homeowners?

Yes, three state programs can lower what an owner pays. The Lottery Credit goes to people who own their home in Wisconsin and lived there as a primary residence on January 1. Apply through the Department of Revenue. Wisconsin sends the county completed applications monthly, and a claim made after the first installment date needs a copy or photo of your latest tax bill uploaded before October 1. A credit stays on the property until the owner or the department removes it.

The Homestead Credit is filed with state income taxes and helps lower-income owners. The Wisconsin Veterans and Surviving Spouses Property Tax Credit can be explored by disabled veterans through the County Veterans Service Office. Owners who struggle to pay can also talk with the County Treasurer about monthly payments, because smaller regular payments reduce the interest that builds up.

What is La Crosse County like?

La Crosse County is the most populous county on Wisconsin's western border, with Minnesota across its western boundary. Its county seat is the city of La Crosse. It was founded in 1851 and covers 480 square miles, of which 452 are land. Neighboring counties are Trempealeau, Jackson, Monroe and Vernon in Wisconsin, plus Houston and Winona counties in Minnesota. The county has two cities, La Crosse and Onalaska, and villages including Bangor, Holmen, Rockland and West Salem.

Freight and passenger rail runs through the county (Amtrak, BNSF and Canadian Pacific), and La Crosse Regional Airport serves it. The climate is continental. July highs average 85.4 degrees Fahrenheit and January highs average 25.9, so heating costs and winter roof condition are fair topics for a buyer's inspection.

Frequently asked questions

When are La Crosse County property taxes due?

They are due in full by January 31, or in two payments by January 31 and July 31. Payments through January 31 go to your municipal treasurer, and later payments go to the La Crosse County Treasurer.

How much interest does La Crosse County charge on late taxes?

The charge is 1 percent a month under Wis. Stat. 74.47 plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty under county ordinance 4.05, counted from February 1. Treasurers cannot waive it for hardship.

Where is the La Crosse County Treasurer's office?

It is in the Administration Center at 212 6th Street North, La Crosse, WI 54601. The phone number is (608) 785-9711, and hours are 8:00 am to 4:30 pm on weekdays.

Who can change my property assessment in La Crosse County?

Only your municipal assessor and, on appeal, the municipal Board of Review can change it. The county's land information office maintains the values the assessor sets. In the City of La Crosse, call the Assessor's Office at 608-789-7525.

How do I remove a deceased spouse's name from a La Crosse County tax bill?

If the home was held in joint tenancy or as survivorship marital property, file a Termination of Decedent's Interest form with the Register of Deeds. If it was held another way, an attorney may need to transfer title, possibly through probate.

Who collects property tax in Vilas County?

Two offices share the work: your town or the City of Eagle River collects the first installment, and the Vilas County Treasurer collects the second installment and every delinquent payment. The treasurer's office is at 330 Court Street in Eagle River, WI 54521, open 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM Monday through Friday, and the phone number is 715-479-3609.

The treasurer's statutory job covers receiving all county money, keeping the financial records, collecting postponed and delinquent real estate taxes and reconciling with the local municipalities. Visitors go through security in the lobby, and the office takes cash, checks, money orders, cashier's checks and debit or credit cards.

The Real Property Listing office in the Land Information Department keeps ownership and parcel descriptions for the county. Reach it at (715) 479-3696 or rpl@vilascountywi.gov. Its online tools include a property tax lookup in the Ascent Land Records Suite with bills from 2020 forward, a legacy lookup for 2011 through 2022 bills, and an opt-out form for owners who do not want their name searchable.

When are Vilas County property taxes due?

The first installment, or the full amount, is due January 31 and goes to the local treasurer. The second installment is due July 31 and goes to the county. Wisconsin taxes real property in two equal installments under Wis. Stat. 74.11, except that a bill under $100 is due in full by January 31.

Under the statute, an installment that is not received within five working days after its due date leaves the entire unpaid amount delinquent: on February 1 for the first installment and on August 1 for the second. Delinquent payments go to the county treasurer, so a late first installment comes to Eagle River. The county starts collecting second installments on February 1.

State law fixes interest on delinquent real estate tax at 1% per month or fraction of a month, and lets a county board add a penalty of up to 0.5% a month (Wis. Stat. 74.47). Ask the treasurer which charges the county applies and what the payoff will be on your closing date.

How can you pay Vilas County property tax?

You can pay in person, by mail, online or by phone, with a few limits on timing. Point and Pay is the county's vendor for online and phone payments, and it only handles delinquent taxes and second installments. The fee is 2.39% for debit and credit cards and $1.50 for an electronic check. The automated phone line, 1-866-518-2304, is closed from December 1 through January 31.

  • By mail: make the check payable to Vilas County Treasurer, write the parcel number on it, and enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope if you want a receipt.
  • Near the deadline: walk the envelope into the post office and ask for a hand postmark. A bank's bill-pay check often arrives without a postmark, and the bank's confirmation does not count as proof of timely payment.
  • In person: bring the parcel number or the tax coupon so the payment lands on the right property.

The county asks owners to send tax bill address changes before November 15, so the bills printed in December reach the right mailbox. The treasurer's page also warns senior homeowners about a property tax scam that the state has publicized.

If you disagree with a value, the next stop is the local board of review. It sits for a 45-day window that starts on the fourth Monday of April, and you must tell the clerk at least 48 hours ahead that you intend to object (Wis. Stat. 70.47). The board treats the assessor's number as correct until your evidence shows otherwise, so bring recent sales or an appraisal.

What tax credit can a Vilas County homeowner claim?

An owner who lives in the house as a primary residence on January 1 may qualify for the Wisconsin lottery and gaming credit, which reduces the bill. The credit does not apply to rentals, vacant land or garages. If it is missing from your bill, the Department of Revenue says to apply to your municipal treasurer by January 31 or file a late claim with the department by October 1.

A second home or cabin does not qualify, because the credit is limited to a primary residence. The credit follows the property when it is sold, so it belongs in the proration at closing, and a buyer who will live there files a new application.

What happens when Vilas County property taxes are not paid?

Vilas County forecloses on tax delinquent property through an in rem tax foreclosure proceeding, which the county treasurer carries out. A seller with unpaid taxes can usually clear the balance from closing proceeds, and under Wis. Stat. 74.51 anyone may discharge delinquent real property taxes with interest and any penalty before a tax certificate issues.

Partial payments of $20 or more are allowed on delinquent taxes under Wis. Stat. 74.49. The county's treasurer collects delinquent taxes all year, so you do not need to wait for a deadline to bring an account current. Request a written payoff that is good through your closing date.

What is Vilas County like for a home seller?

Vilas County is a lake country in Wisconsin's far north, and it is built around tourism and second homes. The county covers 1,018 square miles, of which 857 are land and 161 water, and it holds 1,318 lakes. Large parts of it lie within the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest, the Northern Highland-American Legion State Forest and county forest land. Eagle River is the only city and the county seat. The other 14 communities are towns, and the largest by the 2010 counts in the municipality list are Lac du Flambeau and Arbor Vitae.

The Census Bureau estimated 23,761 residents on July 1, 2025, up 3.1% since April 2020, and 37.1% were 65 or older. For 2020-2024 it reports:

  • A median owner-occupied home value of $300,000, with 84.0% of housing units owner-occupied.
  • Median gross rent of $847 and 2.10 people per household.
  • 11,147 households against 25,498 housing units, a gap that points to seasonal use.
  • 314 building permits in 2025.

Hunting and fishing lead the fall, and ice fishing and snowmobiling lead the winter. Logging, forestry, construction and government round out the local economy. A cabin or lake cottage may sell on a different calendar than a house in town, so ask your agent or buyer how a winter closing affects access, inspections and the second installment due in July.

What should a Vilas County seller ask before listing?

Ask the treasurer for the parcel's tax history and any delinquency, and ask the Real Property Listing office to confirm the name and mailing address on the parcel. If you rent the property to vacationers, the county website lists a Tourist Rooming Houses page under its Business menu. Ask the county what approval carries over to a buyer before you tell anyone the rental income transfers.

Where do I pay my first installment in Vilas County?

Pay it at your local municipality, meaning the town treasurer or the City of Eagle River. The Vilas County Treasurer says timely first-installment and full payments are payable locally, and the county takes the second installment and delinquent payments.

What is the Vilas County Treasurer's address and phone?

The office is at 330 Court Street, Eagle River, WI 54521, and the phone number is 715-479-3609. It is open 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM Monday through Friday, and holiday closures are posted on the county website.

Can I pay Vilas County taxes online?

Yes, for delinquent taxes and second installments. The county uses Point and Pay, which charges 2.39% on debit and credit cards and $1.50 on electronic checks. First installments go to your local municipality, which can tell you whether it has an online option.

How is the Vilas County foreclosure process different?

Vilas County uses an in rem tax foreclosure proceeding for tax delinquent property, and the county treasurer is responsible for it. A delinquent owner can discharge the taxes with interest before a tax certificate issues.

Does the lottery credit carry to the buyer of a Vilas County home?

Yes. The Department of Revenue says the credit stays with the property and should be counted when taxes are prorated. A buyer who will live in the home as a primary residence files a new application.

Who do you pay property tax to in Burnett County, WI?

Pay the first installment to your town or village treasurer, and pay everything after July 31 to the Burnett County Treasurer. The town or village contact information sits in the upper left corner of your tax bill.

That split follows s. 74.11(6), which sends payments made on or before January 31 to the local taxation district treasurer and every other payment to the county treasurer. The County Treasurer's page repeats it in plain terms: current-year real estate taxes by January 31 go to the town or village, and all real estate taxes after July 31 go to Burnett County.

Burnett County has no incorporated cities. Its 24 municipalities are 21 towns (Anderson, Blaine, Daniels, Dewey, Grantsburg, Jackson, LaFollette, Lincoln, Meenon, Oakland, Roosevelt, Rusk, Sand Lake, Scott, Siren, Swiss, Trade Lake, Union, Webb Lake, West Marshland and Wood River) and three villages (Grantsburg, Siren and Webster). Both Grantsburg and Siren appear as a town and as a village, so confirm which one is printed on your bill.

When are Burnett County property taxes due?

Real estate taxes are due January 31, either as a single payment or as the first of two installments, and the second installment is due July 31 (s. 74.11(2)). A bill under $100 must be paid in full by January 31.

  • If a payment is not received within five working days after January 31, the whole unpaid balance is delinquent as of February 1.
  • If the second installment is not received within five working days after July 31, the balance is delinquent as of August 1.
  • When a due date falls on a weekend, the grace period ends at the close of business on the first Friday of the following month.

The next January 31, in 2027, is a Sunday, so the last day to pay on time is Friday, February 5, 2027. July 31, 2027 is a Saturday, which moves that cutoff to Friday, August 6, 2027.

Delinquent real property taxes are paid to the county treasurer, with interest and penalties charged back to the preceding February 1. A municipality may also adopt an ordinance allowing three or more installments, with at least half paid by April 30 and the rest by July 31 (s. 74.12). Look at your bill, or ask your town or village treasurer, to learn which schedule applies to your parcel.

How do you change the mailing address or get payment alerts in Burnett County?

Call the Real Property Lister at 715.349.2183 to change the address that appears on your tax bill. The county treasurer's page lists that number for address change questions.

The county is moving its records to Ascent Land Records software, and the treasurer's page offers a sign-up for text or email notices. The alerts cover four events: your tax bill is ready, a payment has been receipted, a postponement reminder is due, and delinquent taxes are due. Anyone selling a seasonal or inherited home from out of state should sign up so a bill sent to an old address does not go unnoticed.

The office also prepares and mails delinquent tax notices and postponed-tax reminders, issues tax certificates, administers the Lottery and Gaming Credit, and prepares tax settlements.

Who sets your assessment in Burnett County, and how do you appeal it?

Your town's or village's assessor sets your value, and the county is required to carry that value onto the roll. The municipality's page on the county website lists who that is.

A formal appeal goes to the local Board of Review, which meets once a year in a window of 45 days starting on the fourth Monday of April (s. 70.47). In a town, the supervisors and the clerk make up the board unless the town has adopted an ordinance creating another board. A village board uses the village president and clerk in the same way. At least one member must complete state training each year.

  • Tell the board clerk, in writing or orally, at least 48 hours before the first meeting that you plan to object.
  • File a written objection in the first two hours of that meeting. The Department of Revenue form is PA-115A.
  • Show your own estimate of land and improvement value and the information behind it.
  • Expect the board to treat the assessor's number as correct until you present evidence otherwise.

After a Board of Review decision, a court appeal by certiorari must start within 90 days of the notice. An excessive assessment claim under s. 74.37 goes to the municipality by January 31 of the year the tax is payable. The state's Guide for Property Owners covers both steps.

Some parcels are sold over the counter at the County Clerk's office, Room 150 of the Government Center in Siren, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Payment must be cash, check or money order made out to the Burnett County Treasurer. Who handles property tax in Price County, Wisconsin?

Price County property tax is split among town, village and city treasurers, the County Treasurer, the Real Property Lister and a municipal Board of Review. Which office you pay depends on where the house sits. The county seat is Phillips and the largest city is Park Falls, but most of the county is towns.

The Real Property Lister, defined in s. 70.09 of the Wisconsin Statutes, keeps the parcel numbers, ownership taken from the latest document recorded with the Register of Deeds, mailing and property addresses, legal descriptions, assessment rolls and the figures used to print each tax bill. If the name or mailing address on your bill is wrong, that office and the Register of Deeds are where the fix starts. The County Treasurer's page also offers an online property tax search for tax bills, receipts and balance-due statements, updated nightly.

What does Price County look like for a seller?

Price County is a large, thinly settled county in northern Wisconsin: 1,254 square miles of land and 14,054 residents at the 2020 census, with a 2025 estimate of 13,988. All of the population lived in rural areas at the 2020 census, and the median age was 52.8. Timms Hill, the highest natural point in Wisconsin at about 1,951 feet, sits in the Town of Hill, and part of the Chequamegon National Forest lies in the county.

The housing numbers explain why tax bills vary so much from one property to the next. The census counted 10,735 housing units and reported 40.0 percent of them vacant, while 79.6 percent of occupied units were owner-occupied. Price County remains a large producer of raw timber, and the county's tax-rate page lists Managed Forest Land acreage rates alongside ordinary property rates.

  • Towns on the county rate sheet include Catawba, Eisenstein, Elk, Emery, Fifield, Flambeau, Georgetown, Hackett, Harmony, Hill, Kennan, Knox, Lake, Ogema, Prentice, Spirit and Worcester.
  • Villages listed are Catawba, Kennan and Prentice.
  • Cities listed are Park Falls and Phillips.

When are Price County property taxes due, and who collects them?

Most Price County bills follow Wisconsin's default of January 31 and July 31, but six local governments offer a third installment, and the county itself collects every payment for seven others. Bills are mailed by the town, city or village treasurer on or before the third Monday in December. Failing to receive a bill does not remove the duty to pay, so call the municipal treasurer if nothing arrives.

Where the property isWho takes the paymentsInstallment dates
Towns of Catawba, Emery, Lake, Ogema; Village of Prentice; City of PhillipsLocal treasurer through July 31Three installments, with April 30 as the added date
Towns of Fifield, Flambeau, Georgetown, Harmony, Worcester; Villages of Catawba and KennanPrice County Treasurer for all paymentsWisconsin default under s. 74.11 is January 31 and July 31; confirm with the treasurer

The table comes from the County Treasurer's Tax Reminders page, which also says to bring a mailed envelope to the post office for a hand stamp on January 31, April 30 and July 31, since postmarks are now applied at regional centers, often a day or more after mailing. Owners of several parcels should give the tax ID number for each one with a payment.

What does a late payment cost in Price County?

If any single installment is late, the whole unpaid balance becomes delinquent and interest and penalty of 1.5 percent per month run from February 1. The county's own example is that an August balance carries 10.5 percent. The county treasurer says it cannot forgive interest or penalty, because Wis. Stat. s. 74.47 sets the rates and state law allows relief only in narrow cases.

  • A delay or error by the U.S. Postal Service that made a payment arrive late can qualify for relief under s. 74.69.
  • A bankruptcy court sometimes forgives penalty when a bankruptcy is filed.
  • The treasurer accepts monthly payments of $100 or more on unpaid taxes and applies them to the oldest year first.

Under s. 74.11(7), an unpaid first installment is delinquent after the five working day grace period that follows January 31. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff before you set a closing date.

How does tax foreclosure work in Price County?

Price County uses in rem tax foreclosure, and the clock starts September 1. Any current year bill with an unpaid balance on that date receives a tax certificate. If the taxes stay unpaid two years after the certificate date, the county begins a tax deed process with a newspaper publication in April. For delinquent 2023 taxes, the county says that publication comes in April 2027.

Title searches start six months after the publication, and the publication, title search and certified mailing costs are added to the unpaid taxes. That timeline gives an owner behind on a Price County house a real window to sell, but each added fee makes the payoff larger. The county posts the foreclosure notices on its In Rem and Tax Deed Notices page.

The Foundation for Rural Housing, funded in part by the Community Service Block Grant program, is listed by the treasurer for mortgage help, utility help and property tax help when a foreclosure is in process. Its phone is 888-400-5974.

How do you appeal a Price County assessment?

Assessment appeals go to the municipal Board of Review, not the County Treasurer. Under s. 70.47, the clerk must publish notice at least 15 days before the first session, or 30 days if the town, village or city is doing a revaluation. Ask your municipal clerk for the meeting date, because boards in different towns meet on different days.

  • Give the clerk written or oral notice at least 48 hours before the first scheduled meeting, or show good cause for missing it during the first two hours.
  • File a written objection during the first two hours of the first meeting unless the board waives that rule for extraordinary circumstances.
  • Object to the combined value of land and buildings, because an owner of both may not object to only one of them.
  • Be ready to testify under oath and to let the assessor view the property, since refusing a reasonable written request for entry can bar an owner from contesting the assessment.

The Price County website also lists an Assessors and Assessment Codes page and a revaluation primer that explains why a higher assessed value does not always mean a higher bill: what matters is how your increase compares with other properties in the community.

Which credits and rates apply to Price County homes?

The lottery and gaming credit goes to owner-occupied primary residences. If your bill lacks it and you qualify, contact the County Treasurer for a form or use the Department of Revenue lottery credit forms. The county posts its 2025 tax rates, payable in 2026, by town, village or city and school district, so a house in the City of Phillips on the Phillips school district has a different rate from a house in the Town of Prentice on the Prentice district.

Rates come from dividing each levy by total property value. The county and school levies are apportioned to each municipality according to its equalized value, so a town whose values rise faster than its neighbors carries a bigger share of the levy.

Managed Forest Land owners pay an acreage rate. For entries made before 2005, open land is $0.72 per acre and closed land is $1.68. For 2005 and later, open is $1.90 and closed is $9.49. Ask the County Clerk about timber cutting notices if you are selling forest land.

What does the Price County Register of Deeds do for a seller?

The Register of Deeds records and indexes the documents that affect ownership: deeds, easements, mortgages, satisfactions, land contracts, name changes, powers of attorney, federal tax liens, plats and certified survey maps. Documents recorded before September 1951 are not in the searchable computer index, but the office offers copies of the old grantor and grantee indexes and its tract indexes.

The office cannot draft or change a deed, give legal advice, or perform real estate searches. Use a real estate attorney or title company to prepare the deed, and use the State Bar of Wisconsin Lawyer Referral Service if you need one. Statewide rules apply at recording: a recording fee of $30 and a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value, under ss. 59.43 and 77.22. Property Fraud Alert, a free service, sends a phone or email alert when a document is recorded under your name, and the county gives 800-728-3858 as its support line.

How should a Price County owner plan a sale with taxes due?

Start with the parcel's tax search record, then call the treasurer who actually collects your payments, because Price County is split between local collection and county collection. Ask for the current balance, any special charges that sit on the tax roll, and whether an earlier year has a tax certificate. A title company will want the same numbers.

The county also has a Surveyor's Office and a Zoning and Land Conservation office with a shoreland regulations page. Check shoreland rules with Zoning before you promise a buyer a boat house or an addition.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property taxes in Price County?

It depends on the municipality. The county collects all payments for the Towns of Fifield, Flambeau, Georgetown, Harmony and Worcester and the Villages of Catawba and Kennan. Other local treasurers collect through July 31 in places that use three installments.

What is the interest rate on late Price County taxes?

It is 1.5 percent per month, counted from February 1 once an installment is missed. State law sets the rate, and the county treasurer says it may not forgive interest or penalty outside narrow cases.

How long before Price County starts tax foreclosure?

The county issues a tax certificate on bills unpaid September 1. If the taxes remain unpaid two years after that date, the county starts the process with a publication in April, then title searches six months later.

Where do I appeal my Price County property assessment?

File with your municipal Board of Review. The clerk publishes the meeting notice, and you need to give notice at least 48 hours ahead and file a written objection within the first two hours of the first meeting.

Can the Price County Register of Deeds write my deed?

No. The office records documents but cannot draft or change a deed or give legal advice. Use an attorney or title company, then record the signed deed with the $30 fee plus the 30-cents-per-$100 transfer fee.

Who collects property tax in Kenosha County?

Your local municipality collects the first payment, and the Kenosha County Treasurer takes over after the local deadline passes. The Treasurer's Office is at 1010 56th Street, Kenosha, WI 53140, phone 262-653-2542. It administers the property tax laws, collects delinquent taxes, and settles each year with the county's municipalities, school districts, Gateway Technical College and the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.

Walk-in payments for second and later installments and for delinquent taxes go to the downtown office on 56th Street (8 am to 5 pm, Monday through Friday) or to the Elected Officials Office at the Kenosha County Center, at the intersection of Highways 45 and 50 in Bristol (8 am to 4:30 pm, Monday through Friday). Under Wis. Stat. 74.11(6), payments made on or before January 31 go to the municipal treasurer, and all other payments go to the county treasurer unless your bill says otherwise.

The county's Property & Taxes page links to a Property Inquiry portal where you can see tax bills, assessments, sales and building data for a parcel, plus current and historical county mill rates.

When are Kenosha County property taxes due?

The full amount or the first installment is due on or before January 31. Where the second installment goes depends on the municipality, as the table shows.

Where the parcel isInstallmentsPay to
City of KenoshaFull payment, or three installments due Jan 31, Apr 30 and Jul 31City of Kenosha through July 31
Village of Pleasant PrairieFull payment, or three installments due Jan 31, Apr 30 and Jul 31Village of Pleasant Prairie through July 31
All other municipalitiesFull payment or first installment by Jan 31Local town or village treasurer for Jan 31; Kenosha County Treasurer for the second installment and anything delinquent

Source: Kenosha County Property Tax Payments page.

Bills are mailed in mid-December. State law (74.09(5)) sets the mailing deadline at the third Monday in December, which is December 21 in 2026. If nothing has arrived by about December 20, call your municipal treasurer. Under 74.09(6), a missing bill does not excuse a late payment.

The 2026 first-installment date, January 31, 2027, falls on a Sunday. Under 74.11(7)(b) and 74.12(7)(b), when January 31 lands on a weekend the five-working-day window runs through the first Friday in February, which is February 5, 2027. Confirm the exact cutoff with your treasurer before relying on it.

What happens if I miss a Kenosha County tax payment?

The whole unpaid balance becomes delinquent and the installment option ends. If the first installment is missed, the entire remaining tax is delinquent as of February 1 (74.11(7) and 74.12(7)). If the July 31 installment is missed, the unpaid balance is delinquent as of August 1, and interest and penalty are charged back to February 1.

The rate is 1 percent per month under 74.47(1), with a fraction of a month counted as a whole month, plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty that a county can add by ordinance under 74.47(2). Kenosha County lists the combined charge as 18 percent a year. The county treasurer's FAQ also says state law sets these amounts and the office cannot adjust them.

Prior-year delinquent taxes are always payable at the County Treasurer's Office. The county will set up a payment plan with these terms:

  • Prior-year taxes must be paid within 10 months for each delinquent year, so one year gets 10 months and two years get 20.
  • Three years in delinquent status starts the tax deed foreclosure process, and the property can be lost.
  • Current-year installments must also be paid on time during the plan.
  • Missing a plan payment, or letting current-year taxes go delinquent, cancels the plan and makes the whole balance due. The FAQ says two missed plan payments cancel it.

Owners in the City of Kenosha or Pleasant Prairie who fall behind on current-year taxes should call their local treasurer before July 31 and the County Treasurer after that date.

How do I pay Kenosha County property tax?

The county accepts several methods, and a few details matter for mail and online payments.

  • Mail: send your payment with the stub from the top of the bill. If you want a receipt, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope. Near a deadline, take the envelope to the post office and ask for a hand postmark. A bank's bill-pay check often has no postmark, and the bank's confirmation does not prove timely payment.
  • In person: cash, check, money order or cashier's check at either county office. Credit cards are also accepted.
  • Online: through the Property Inquiry portal with the 13-digit parcel identification number from your bill. Credit card transactions carry a fee, and electronic check is also offered.
  • Phone: 1-888-891-6064, extension 2.

Under 74.69(1), a payment is timely if it is in a properly addressed envelope, postmarked on or before the due date with postage prepaid, and received within five working days after the due date. Owners with a mortgage escrow remain responsible for the tax. The county recommends checking that the lender actually paid it, and it advises against asking that all notices go to the mortgage company.

How do I challenge a Kenosha County assessment?

Assessments are set by the municipality where the property sits, and the appeal starts there. Each municipality's Board of Review meets once a year during the 45-day window that begins on the fourth Monday in April, and no sooner than 7 days after the assessment roll closes for examination (70.47(1)). The clerk must publish notice at least 15 days before the first session, or 30 days before in a revaluation year (70.47(2)).

To be heard, give the board clerk written or oral notice of intent to object at least 48 hours before the first meeting. Then file the written objection within the first two hours of that meeting (70.47(7)(a)). A person who owns land and improvements can object only to the combined value. If you disagree with the board's decision, the next step is an action for certiorari in court, which must start within 90 days after you receive the board's notice (70.47(13)).

The 2026 sessions are over. To prepare for 2027, ask your municipal assessor when open book is scheduled and which clerk handles Board of Review filings.

What credits and relief programs apply in Kenosha County?

The Wisconsin Lottery and Gaming Credit goes to owners whose home was their primary residence on January 1. The county's Property & Taxes page has a Lottery Credit search so you can verify you receive it, and the county treasurer can send an application, as can your municipal treasurer. The WI County Treasurers Association explains that a lottery credit stays with the property until the owner or the Department of Revenue removes it, and that a late claim after the first installment date needs a copy of your latest tax bill uploaded before October 1.

The same association's FAQ points lower-income owners to the Homestead Credit filed with state income taxes. It points disabled veterans to the Wisconsin Veterans and Surviving Spouses Property Tax Credit through the County Veterans Service Office. The treasurer cannot forgive interest for hardship.

How are property taxes handled when I sell in Kenosha County?

Taxes for the sale year are usually split between seller and buyer in the purchase contract. If the contract says nothing, Wis. Stat. 74.15 makes the seller pay the buyer one-twelfth of the prior year's taxes for each month elapsed before the conveyance, counting the sale month when the deed date falls after the 15th. Taxes paid in advance of the levy are accepted by the municipal treasurer from August 1 until the third Monday in December (74.13), which gives a seller who wants the year settled a way to prepay.

If the parcel is delinquent, the payoff comes from the County Treasurer, and it includes interest and penalty through the closing date. Ask the treasurer's office at 262-653-2542 for a written figure good through the day you expect to close. Special assessments and special charges on the bill are collected the same way as the tax, and a missed special charge can make the whole parcel delinquent (74.11(10)(b)).

What is Kenosha County like for homeowners?

Kenosha County sits in the southeast corner of Wisconsin on the western shore of Lake Michigan, with Racine County to the north, Walworth County to the west, and Lake and McHenry counties in Illinois to the south. It was formed from Racine County on January 30, 1850. Its land area is 271.8 square miles, and Metra's Union Pacific North Line links it to Chicago.

The Census Bureau estimated 168,448 residents in 2025, which makes it the eighth most populous Wisconsin county. For 2020 to 2024 the median owner-occupied home value is $265,500, 66.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied, median household income is $81,239 and median gross rent is $1,219. The county issued 892 building permits in 2025. Besides the City of Kenosha, the county includes villages such as Pleasant Prairie, Bristol, Paddock Lake, Salem Lakes and Twin Lakes, and towns such as Brighton, Paris, Randall and Wheatland.

Frequently asked questions

When are Kenosha County property taxes due?

The full amount or the first installment is due by January 31. Second installments go to the County Treasurer after that, except in the City of Kenosha and Village of Pleasant Prairie, which collect three installments (Jan 31, Apr 30, Jul 31) and keep current-year payments through July 31.

What interest does Kenosha County charge on late property tax?

Delinquent tax carries 1 percent interest per month under Wis. Stat. 74.47(1) plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty, which the county lists as 18 percent a year. The charge runs back to February 1 and cannot be waived by the treasurer.

Can I get a payment plan for delinquent Kenosha County taxes?

Yes. The County Treasurer sets up plans for prior-year taxes, requiring payment within 10 months for each delinquent year and on-time current-year installments. Three years of delinquency starts tax deed foreclosure.

Where do I pay Kenosha County property tax online?

Use the Property Inquiry portal linked from the county's Property & Taxes page. You need the 13-digit parcel number from your bill, and credit card payments carry a fee. For City of Kenosha parcels, current-year payments through July 31 go to the city, not the county.

How do I appeal my Kenosha County assessment?

Contact your municipal assessor first, then file with the municipal Board of Review. Give notice of intent at least 48 hours before the first meeting and file the written objection in the first two hours (Wis. Stat. 70.47(7)(a)). Court review by certiorari must start within 90 days of the board's notice.
